Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

vignette:
Mai was forty-eight when she finally walked into a clinic, though she had been living with the aftermath for nearly two years. The stalking had started subtly-a customer at the restaurant where she waited tables who began coming in every shift, sitting in her section, leaving notes folded under the plate. She had dismissed it at first, told herself she was being paranoid, that he was just lonely. But then he started waiting for her in the parking lot, and she began taking different routes home, checking her rearview mirror obsessively. The night it escalated, he followed her all the way to her apartment complex and stood outside her door for hours, knocking softly, whispering her name. She called the police, got a restraining order, but by then the damage was done.

What Mai could not shake was how the memory felt-it would surge into her mind without warning, a sudden, visceral flood of that hallway, the sound of his voice through the wood, the smell of the cheap cologne he wore. She could not put it into words when her sister asked what happened; the event felt like a series of images and sensations that belonged to someone else, a story she had heard rather than lived. Because she could not speak it, because it felt alien and unreal, she began to believe that she was simply broken, that the person she used to be-the one who laughed easily, who found joy in small things-had been replaced by someone hollow. She had lost her happiness, she was certain of that, and nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. She felt dead inside, and this emptiness became the lens through which she saw everything.

It was this belief-that she was fundamentally changed, emptied out-that drove her avoidance. She stopped seeing friends she had socialized with before the event, certain they would see the misery in her and pull away. She avoided any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, because she was convinced she no longer had the emotional reserves to handle conflict, that one sharp word would shatter her completely. She also began paying unusual attention to her own body, scanning herself for signs of tension or weakness, as if monitoring a machine she no longer trusted.

The threat never left her. At home, she listened constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering-the creak of a floorboard, the click of a lock, the whisper of fabric. She avoided unfamiliar places entirely, reasoning that she could not assess the danger in a space she did not know. Her body reacted before her mind could catch up: a sudden noise, a car door slamming, and her heart would pound, her hands would shake, her breath would come too fast. These physical reactions only deepened her conviction that she was no longer safe in the world, that her own nervous system was a traitor.

And because she avoided so much-because she stayed home, stayed silent, stayed small-the memories came more often. Without the distraction of work or conversation or the simple act of walking through a new street, there was nothing to interrupt the intrusion. The memory would force its way in while she was washing dishes, while she was trying to fall asleep, while she was standing at the stove stirring soup. Each time it came, it reinforced her belief that she was trapped, that she would never feel again, that the person she had been was gone. The cycle tightened: the emptiness drove her to avoid, the avoidance left her alone with the threat, the threat made the memories worse, and the memories deepened the emptiness.

She had stopped going to the restaurant altogether after six months. Her manager had been understanding at first, but eventually the shifts stopped being held. She lived on savings and then on credit, and she told herself she would go back when she felt better, but she never did. What finally brought her to the clinic was a night when she found herself standing in her kitchen at 3 a.m., listening to the refrigerator hum, and she realized she could not remember the last time she had spoken to anyone. She was afraid that this was all that was left-that the woman she had been was not coming back. But she was also afraid that if she tried to reach for her, she would find only more emptiness.
